Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on the central cornea. Seidel test is negative. There is no retained foreign body visible on slit lamp examination or eversion of the upper lid.
winner_protocol:
Age: 30 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in the left eye after a metallic foreign body struck the eye during metal grinding without safety goggles. Associated photophobia, difficulty keeping the eye open, and blurriness attributed to tearing.
Analysis: The clinical picture is consistent with a simple traumatic corneal abrasion of the left eye. The history of metal grinding, acute onset of sharp pain, tearing, photophobia, and the finding of a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on fluorescein staining with a negative Seidel test and no visible retained foreign body on slit lamp examination or lid eversion support this diagnosis. The absence of hypopyon, hyphema, and a round reactive pupil argue against open globe or intraocular involvement. Differential considerations include retained corneal foreign body, corneal laceration or open globe (ruled out by negative Seidel test), infectious keratitis (especially given contact lens use), recurrent corneal erosion, and chemical injury (unlikely given the mechanism). The condition is urgent but not immediately sight-threatening; it can be managed initially in urgent care with appropriate follow-up.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Slit lamp examination with fluorescein staining and Seidel test have already been performed. No additional imaging or laboratory tests are indicated for this uncomplicated presentation. A careful slit lamp examination, including double lid eversion or sweeping of the fornices with a cotton-tipped applicator, may be considered to definitively rule out a retained foreign body.
Conclusion: Simple corneal abrasion of the left eye, likely due to a metallic foreign body strike, with no evidence of open globe, retained foreign body, or intraocular infection. This is a non-emergent condition that requires prompt evaluation and management, with ophthalmology follow-up to ensure healing and detect complications.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology
Recommendations: Prescribe topical antibiotic ointment or drops (e.g., erythromycin or a fluoroquinolone) to prevent infection. Consider a cycloplegic agent (e.g., homatropine) for pain relief from ciliary spasm. Provide oral analgesics as needed. Do not patch the eye, especially in contact lens wearers, due to increased infection risk. Avoid topical anesthetics for pain control as they can delay healing and cause corneal toxicity. Assess tetanus prophylaxis status and update if not current. Instruct the patient to avoid contact lens wear until the eye is fully healed and cleared by an ophthalmologist. Advise the patient to return immediately if pain worsens, vision decreases, or if discharge or redness increases. Schedule follow-up with ophthalmology within 24-48 hours to confirm healing and rule out complications. Provide occupational safety counseling; advise always wearing appropriate eye protection when grinding metal. Reassess visual acuity after healing to confirm return to baseline (20/20).
Notes: Contact lens use increases the risk of bacterial keratitis, especially Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and should be considered in the differential and management. The linear epithelial defect may suggest an expelled foreign body or a rust ring; careful slit lamp examination is needed. Consider the possibility of recurrent corneal erosion if the patient has a history of previous abrasions. Consider the possibility of a contact lens-induced abrasion, but the history of trauma is more consistent with a traumatic abrasion.

Diagnosis10: Embolism and thrombosis of arteries of lower extremities
Vignette: A 68-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe pain, coldness, and numbness in his left leg that started approximately 3 hours ago while sitting at home. He has a history of atrial fibrillation and was recently taken off warfarin due to a GI bleed. On examination, the left leg is pale and cool to the touch from the mid-thigh distally. Vital signs: T 36.9C, HR 88 (irregularly irregular), RR 16, BP 148/86, SpO2 97%. Left dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent by palpation and Doppler. Left popliteal pulse is faintly detectable. The left calf is tender with decreased sensation and the patient is unable to dorsiflex or plantarflex the left foot. Right leg pulses are palpable and symmetric. CT angiography shows abrupt occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery.

Vignette:
A 68-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe pain, coldness, and numbness in his left leg that started approximately 3 hours ago while sitting at home. He has a history of atrial fibrillation and was recently taken off warfarin due to a GI bleed. On examination, the left leg is pale and cool to the touch from the mid-thigh distally. Vital signs: T 36.9C, HR 88 (irregularly irregular), RR 16, BP 148/86, SpO2 97%. Left dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent by palpation and Doppler. Left popliteal pulse is faintly detectable. The left calf is tender with decreased sensation and the patient is unable to dorsiflex or plantarflex the left foot. Right leg pulses are palpable and symmetric. CT angiography shows abrupt occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery.

Age: 68
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sudden onset of severe pain, coldness, and numbness in the left leg beginning approximately 3 hours prior to presentation while sitting at home, in a patient with a history of atrial fibrillation who was recently taken off warfarin due to a gastrointestinal bleed.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is consistent with acute limb ischemia of the left leg due to abrupt occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery, most likely embolic in origin given the history of atrial fibrillation and recent cessation of anticoagulation. Strong supporting findings include sudden onset of severe pain, pallor, coolness, absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses by palpation and Doppler, a faintly detectable popliteal pulse, and the presence of both sensory (decreased sensation) and motor (inability to dorsiflex or plantarflex the foot) deficits. CT angiography confirms the occlusion site. The motor and sensory deficits indicate advanced ischemia (Rutherford category IIb) with risk of irreversible tissue damage within 4–6 hours. Main differential considerations include acute arterial thrombosis in situ, aortic dissection with limb involvement, deep vein thrombosis (phlegmasia cerulea dolens), vasospasm, and trauma; however, the CT angiography finding of abrupt occlusion in the setting of atrial fibrillation strongly favors embolic occlusion.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Complete blood count; coagulation profile (PT/INR, aPTT); serum electrolytes; renal function (creatinine); creatine kinase; lactate; ECG to confirm atrial fibrillation; echocardiography (including transesophageal echocardiography) to identify a cardiac embolic source; Doppler ultrasound for pulse assessment; continuous monitoring equipment for compartment syndrome and reperfusion injury.
Conclusion: This is a limb-threatening surgical emergency. The patient has acute limb ischemia of the left leg due to embolic occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery, likely from atrial fibrillation, with motor and sensory deficits indicating severe ischemia. Immediate revascularization is required to prevent irreversible tissue loss and limb loss. The recent GI bleed complicates anticoagulation but limb salvage remains the priority.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Initiate immediate systemic anticoagulation with intravenous heparin, with careful risk-benefit assessment given the recent GI bleed; the risk of limb loss outweighs bleeding risk, and the decision should be individualized with vascular surgery. Provide adequate pain control. Consult vascular surgery (or general surgery if vascular surgery is unavailable) urgently for revascularization via surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed thrombolysis, ideally within 6 hours of symptom onset. After revascularization, monitor closely for compartment syndrome (consider calf pressure monitoring) and reperfusion injury, including hyperkalemia, acidosis, and acute kidney injury; monitor renal function and potassium levels. Assess for other embolic phenomena (renal, mesenteric, or cerebral) given the embolic source. Obtain baseline renal function and electrolytes before contrast administration and during reperfusion therapy. After the acute event, plan long-term anticoagulation (e.g., warfarin or DOAC) for atrial fibrillation with gastroenterology input to manage GI bleed risk. Consider alternative embolic sources (e.g., aortic or popliteal aneurysm) and perform thorough cardiac evaluation, including transesophageal echocardiography, to rule out left atrial thrombus or other cardiac sources.
Notes: The recent GI bleed significantly complicates anticoagulation; the risk of recurrent embolism must be weighed against rebleeding risk. Motor deficit (inability to move the foot) indicates severe ischemia (Rutherford category IIb) and mandates immediate surgical consultation; revascularization should not be delayed beyond 6 hours. Faint popliteal pulse suggests proximal occlusion with possible collateral flow, but urgent intervention is still critical. Consider the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy from CT angiography, especially with potential dehydration and underlying renal impairment.

Vignette:
An 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after pulling a pot of boiling water off the stove onto himself approximately 45 minutes ago. He sustained scald burns to his anterior chest, abdomen, both upper extremities, and portions of his face. He has been crying inconsolably. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, he is alert but in severe pain and distress. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 152, RR 28, BP 94/58, SpO2 98%. Weight is 28 kg. Burns cover approximately 20% total body surface area: areas of erythema with large intact and ruptured blisters (superficial partial thickness) on the chest and abdomen, with waxy white insensate areas (deep partial to full thickness) on both forearms. No circumferential burns are identified. Facial burns are superficial with no singed nasal hairs and no evidence of inhalation injury. He has no hoarseness or stridor. Parkland formula is calculated (20% TBSA x 28 kg x 4 mL = 2,240 mL LR over first 24 hours), IV access is obtained, and morphine is administered for pain.

Age: 8 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Scald burns to the anterior chest, abdomen, both upper extremities, and portions of the face after pulling a pot of boiling water onto himself approximately 45 minutes prior to presentation. The patient is in severe pain and distress.
Analysis: The patient sustained a thermal scald injury covering approximately 20% total body surface area (TBSA) with mixed depth: superficial partial-thickness burns (erythema with intact and ruptured blisters) on the chest and abdomen, and deep partial-to-full-thickness burns (waxy white, insensate areas) on both forearms. Facial burns are superficial with no singed nasal hairs, hoarseness, or stridor, and there is no evidence of inhalation injury. No circumferential burns are identified. The patient is tachycardic (HR 152) and hypertensive (BP 94/58) with a normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation, consistent with pain and early fluid shifts. Burns greater than 10% TBSA in a child are considered major and require emergent care. The strongest supporting facts are the clear mechanism of injury, the calculated 20% TBSA, the presence of deep burns on both forearms, and the need for fluid resuscitation. The primary diagnosis is accidental scald burn. Differential considerations include other causes of blistering skin lesions such as toxic epidermal necrolysis, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, or chemical burns, but the history of hot water spill makes scald burn the clear diagnosis. Non-accidental injury (child abuse) should be considered if the history is inconsistent with the injury pattern.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: No specific laboratory or imaging studies are immediately indicated. Clinical assessment with accurate TBSA calculation, continuous vital sign monitoring, and hourly urine output monitoring (target 1–1.5 mL/kg/hr in children) are required. Tetanus status should be checked and prophylaxis updated if not current. Baseline labs (CBC, electrolytes, BUN/creatinine) may be obtained for monitoring fluid and electrolyte balance, though not explicitly required by the case. Carboxyhemoglobin level is not indicated given no evidence of inhalation injury.
Conclusion: This is an 8-year-old boy with a 20% TBSA mixed-depth scald burn requiring emergent stabilization, fluid resuscitation per the Parkland formula (2,240 mL Lactated Ringer's over 24 hours, with half in the first 8 hours from the time of burn), adequate pain control, wound care, and close monitoring for complications including hypovolemic shock, compartment syndrome, and delayed airway compromise. Transfer to a pediatric burn center is likely indicated for specialized care.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations:
- Continue IV fluid resuscitation with Lactated Ringer's per the Parkland formula: 2,240 mL over 24 hours, with half (1,120 mL) given in the first 8 hours from the time of burn and the remainder over the next 16 hours. Add maintenance fluids for children in addition to the Parkland formula.
- Administer adequate pain control with morphine and reassess frequently; consider anxiolysis for distress.
- Perform wound care: gentle cleaning, debridement of ruptured blisters, and application of topical antimicrobials (e.g., silver sulfadiazine) for partial-thickness burns. Deep burns on the forearms may require surgical evaluation for possible excision and grafting.
- Monitor hourly urine output (target 1–1.5 mL/kg/hr) and vital signs to guide fluid resuscitation and detect hypovolemic shock.
- Monitor for compartment syndrome, especially on both forearms, despite the absence of circumferential burns; if neurovascular compromise develops, consider escharotomy.
- Monitor for delayed airway compromise from facial burns, even though no inhalation injury is currently present.
- Monitor for hypothermia, especially in children with large burns; keep the patient warm.
- Update tetanus prophylaxis if not current.
- Consider non-accidental injury (child abuse) if the history is inconsistent with the injury pattern.
- Consult a pediatric burn center or pediatric surgery for ongoing management and likely transfer.
- Provide nutritional support and metabolic monitoring for large burns.
- Provide psychological support for the child and family.
- Ensure accurate weight for fluid calculations.
Notes: The deep partial-to-full-thickness burns on both forearms carry a risk of compartment syndrome; serial neurovascular checks are essential. Facial burns can cause airway edema, so monitor for delayed respiratory compromise. Children require maintenance fluids in addition to the Parkland formula. None.

Age: 29
Sex: Female
Complaint: An 8-month history of near-constant, excessive worry across multiple life domains (work performance, finances, health, children's safety), with an inability to control the worry despite recognizing it as disproportionate. Associated symptoms include restlessness, neck and shoulder muscle tension, difficulty falling asleep, irritability, and difficulty concentrating during meetings. The patient has tried meditation and exercise with only partial benefit.
Analysis: The clinical presentation meets DSM-5 criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD): excessive anxiety and worry present for more days than not for at least 6 months (here, 8 months) across multiple domains, difficulty controlling the worry, and associated symptoms including restlessness, muscle tension, sleep disturbance, irritability, and impaired concentration. The GAD-7 score of 16 indicates severe anxiety, and the physical finding of bilateral trapezius muscle tightness is consistent with the reported muscle tension. Normal thyroid function tests rule out hyperthyroidism, a common medical mimic. The patient denies panic attacks, specific phobias, obsessive thoughts, and trauma, narrowing the differential away from panic disorder, specific phobia, OCD, and PTSD. Other differential considerations include major depressive disorder (no core depressive symptoms are mentioned, but comorbidity must be screened), social anxiety disorder, and substance-induced anxiety (caffeine use is minimal at one cup daily, but should be considered). The presentation is chronic and stable, with normal vital signs and no acute distress, suicidal ideation, or medical instability, indicating a non-emergent situation.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Screening for comorbid depression (e.g., PHQ-9) and a detailed substance use history (including alcohol and illicit drugs; urine toxicology if substance-induced anxiety is suspected). A 40-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of persistent nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, and clear rhinorrhea. She notes that symptoms are present year-round but worsen when she vacuums or dusts her home. She denies any history of asthma, wheezing, or shortness of breath. She has tried over-the-counter antihistamines intermittently with partial relief. On examination, nasal mucosa is pale and boggy bilaterally. There is a transverse nasal crease. winner_protocol:
Age: 40 years

Sex: Female

Complaint: Persistent nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, and clear rhinorrhea for 2 years; symptoms are year-round but worsen with vacuuming or dusting; partial relief with over-the-counter antihistamines.

Analysis: The clinical picture is classic for perennial allergic rhinitis, most likely due to dust mite allergy. Supporting findings include year-round symptoms worsened by dust exposure, pale and boggy nasal mucosa bilaterally, a transverse nasal crease (indicating chronic nasal rubbing), clear rhinorrhea, and partial response to antihistamines. The absence of asthma, wheezing, and abnormal lung auscultation, along with no visualized nasal polyps, argues against significant lower airway involvement or polyp disease. The older home with carpeted bedrooms and no pets further implicates dust mites as the primary allergen. Main differential considerations include non-allergic (vasomotor) rhinitis, chronic rhinosinusitis, nasal polyps (not visualized but not fully excluded), rhinitis medicamentosa (if decongestant sprays are overused), and structural nasal abnormalities. Red flags such as unilateral symptoms, bloody discharge, crusting, facial pain, anosmia, or systemic symptoms are absent, confirming a non-urgent, chronic condition.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Allergy testing (skin prick test or specific IgE) to confirm sensitization, particularly to dust mites; nasal endoscopy if polyps or other structural abnormalities are suspected despite normal anterior rhinoscopy.

Conclusion: The patient has perennial allergic rhinitis, likely dust mite allergy, presenting as a chronic, stable condition without acute complications. The diagnosis is strongly supported by history and physical examination, and the condition is manageable with allergen avoidance and appropriate medical therapy. No emergency intervention is required.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)

Recommendations: Initiate a stepwise management plan. Emphasize environmental control measures for dust mites: encase pillows and mattresses in allergen-proof covers, wash bedding in hot water weekly, remove or reduce carpeting (especially in bedrooms), and consider HEPA filters. Prescribe an intranasal corticosteroid (e.g., fluticasone) as first-line therapy, with a second-generation oral antihistamine for breakthrough symptoms; saline nasal irrigation may be added for symptom relief. Confirm the patient is not overusing OTC decongestant sprays to rule out rhinitis medicamentosa. Assess pregnancy status before prescribing medications, as it may alter treatment choices. Evaluate for coexisting atopic conditions such as allergic conjunctivitis or eczema, and inquire about occupational exposures if symptoms persist. Monitor for the future development of asthma, as allergic rhinitis is a risk factor, even though the patient currently denies respiratory symptoms. Schedule follow-up in 4–6 weeks to assess response and adherence; if symptoms are refractory despite adherence, consider referral to ENT or Allergy/Immunology for allergen immunotherapy after confirming sensitization. Discuss the impact of symptoms on quality of life and sleep, as this may influence treatment intensity.

Notes: The transverse nasal crease is a supportive sign of chronic nasal rubbing and reinforces the allergic etiology. Although no nasal polyps were visualized on anterior rhinoscopy, nasal endoscopy should be considered if symptoms are atypical or refractory. The minor divergence regarding initial management setting (primary care vs. ENT) does not change the overall plan; ENT referral is appropriate given the consensus specialization and the partial response to prior antihistamine therapy.

- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.

First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,

Vignette:
A 16-year-old female high school student presents with complaints of fever, sore throat, and fatigue. She started feeling sick 1 week ago. Her symptoms are gradually getting worse, and she has difficulty swallowing. She has had a fever every day, and she could hardly get out of bed this morning. She does not remember being exposed to anybody with a similar illness recently. On physical examination she is febrile and looks sick. Enlarged cervical lymph nodes, exudative pharyngitis with soft palate petechiae and faint erythematous macular rash on the trunk and arms are found.
winner_protocol:
Age: 16 years

Sex: Female

Complaint: Fever, sore throat, fatigue, and difficulty swallowing, progressively worsening over one week, with inability to get out of bed on the day of presentation.

Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus infection). Strong supporting findings include the combination of fever, exudative pharyngitis with soft palate petechiae, enlarged cervical lymph nodes, severe fatigue, and a faint erythematous macular rash on the trunk and arms in an adolescent. The gradual onset over one week, daily fevers, and prostration further support this diagnosis. The absence of known exposure does not rule out EBV. Main differential considerations include group A streptococcal pharyngitis, acute HIV infection, cytomegalovirus (CMV), toxoplasmosis, and other viral pharyngitides (e.g., adenovirus, influenza). Streptococcal pharyngitis is a common bacterial cause that must be excluded because it requires specific antibiotic treatment. The presence of palatal petechiae and a macular rash, together with lymphadenopathy and fatigue, strongly favors EBV over streptococcal infection. The patient's sick appearance, difficulty swallowing, and inability to get out of bed raise concern for complications such as airway compromise from tonsillar enlargement, dehydration, or splenic rupture, warranting emergent evaluation.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Complete blood count with differential (looking for lymphocytosis and atypical lymphocytes); heterophile antibody test (Monospot); EBV-specific serology (VCA IgM and IgG) if Monospot is negative; throat culture or rapid antigen test for group A streptococcus; liver function tests. Consider abdominal ultrasound if splenomegaly is palpable or symptomatic.

Conclusion: The most likely diagnosis is acute infectious mononucleosis due to Epstein-Barr virus infection. The patient requires emergent care because she looks sick, has difficulty swallowing, and has been febrile for a week with significant fatigue, raising concern for complications such as airway compromise or dehydration. Management is primarily supportive, with specific precautions to prevent splenic rupture and avoidance of ampicillin/amoxicillin due to the risk of rash.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease

Recommendations: 
- Evaluate urgently in an emergency setting to assess for airway compromise (stridor, drooling, severe dysphagia), dehydration, and splenic rupture (sudden abdominal pain, left shoulder pain, lightheadedness).
- Assess hydration status and ability to swallow; consider IV fluids if dehydrated.
- Perform serial examinations to monitor tonsillar enlargement and airway patency.
- Assess for splenomegaly on examination; consider abdominal ultrasound if palpable or symptomatic.
- Order initial tests: CBC with differential, Monospot, EBV-specific serology (VCA IgM/IgG) if Monospot negative, throat culture or rapid strep test, and liver function tests.
- Provide supportive care: rest, adequate hydration, and analgesics/antipyretics (acetaminophen or ibuprofen) for fever and throat pain. Avoid NSAIDs if there is concern for bleeding or thrombocytopenia.
- Do not administer antibiotics unless streptococcal co-infection is confirmed; if antibiotics are needed, avoid ampicillin/amoxicillin due to the high risk of rash in mononucleosis.
- Corticosteroids are reserved for complications such as airway compromise or severe tonsillar hypertrophy.
- Advise avoidance of contact sports and heavy lifting for at least 3-4 weeks (some experts recommend 4-6 weeks) due to splenic enlargement risk.
- Inquire about recent antibiotic use (especially amoxicillin/ampicillin) to explain the rash.
- Consider sexual history and pregnancy testing in this sexually active adolescent.
- Consider immunocompromised status, as it may alter the presentation.
- Educate the patient and family about contagiousness and hygiene.
- Provide return precautions: return immediately for worsening abdominal pain, breathing difficulty, or inability to swallow fluids.
- Arrange follow-up to monitor for complications, especially splenomegaly and liver function abnormalities; symptoms typically resolve over 2-4 weeks, but fatigue may persist for months.

Notes: Expert C classified the condition as non-emergent, noting no immediate life-threatening features such as stridor or sepsis, but recommended prompt evaluation within 24-48 hours; the consensus label of "Requires emergent care" reflects the majority expert vote given the patient's sick appearance and progressive symptoms. Expert C recommended a longer activity restriction period of 4-6 weeks compared to the 3-4 weeks suggested by others; the longer period may be considered for safety.

Vignette:
A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his parents after 6 hours of rapidly progressive sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and noisy breathing. He has had no significant past medical history and immunizations are not up to date (parents declined some vaccines). On examination, the child is sitting upright in a tripod position, leaning forward with his neck extended and jaw thrust forward. He is drooling profusely and appears anxious and toxic-appearing. Vital signs: T 39.8C, HR 162, RR 34, SpO2 92% on room air. Inspiratory stridor is audible without a stethoscope. His voice is muffled and he refuses to speak or drink. A soft tissue lateral neck X-ray obtained reveals a thumb sign consistent with epiglottic swelling. Anesthesiology and ENT are urgently called for airway management.
winner_protocol:
Age: 4 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: A 4-year-old boy presents with 6 hours of rapidly progressive sore throat, difficulty swallowing, noisy breathing, profuse drooling, muffled voice, inspiratory stridor, high fever, and hypoxia (SpO2 92% on room air), sitting in a tripod position and appearing anxious and toxic.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for acute epiglottitis (supraglottitis). Strongest supporting facts include the acute onset of symptoms, high fever (39.8°C), tripod positioning with neck extended and jaw thrust forward, profuse drooling, muffled voice, inspiratory stridor audible without a stethoscope, toxic appearance, and hypoxia. The soft tissue lateral neck X-ray showing a thumb sign consistent with epiglottic swelling confirms the diagnosis. The child's incomplete immunization status increases the risk of Haemophilus influenzae type b infection, a classic cause of epiglottitis. This is a life-threatening airway emergency with impending complete airway obstruction. Main differential considerations include croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), bacterial tracheitis, retropharyngeal abscess, foreign body aspiration, peritonsillar abscess, and angioedema; however, the thumb sign and toxic appearance strongly favor epiglottitis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Lateral neck X-ray (already obtained and diagnostic); no further imaging should delay airway management. After the airway is secured, obtain blood cultures and epiglottic cultures to guide antibiotic therapy. Prepare difficult airway equipment including endotracheal tubes of various sizes, laryngoscope, and surgical airway equipment (cricothyrotomy/tracheostomy) in the operating room or ICU.
Conclusion: This is acute epiglottitis, a life-threatening airway emergency requiring immediate airway management by anesthesiology and ENT, followed by empiric antibiotics and supportive care. With prompt intervention, the prognosis is good, but delayed management can lead to complete airway obstruction, respiratory arrest, anoxic brain injury, sepsis, pneumonia, or epiglottic abscess.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations:
1. Secure the airway immediately in a controlled setting (operating room or ICU) with anesthesiology and ENT present; use endotracheal intubation or surgical airway if needed. Do not delay airway management for any other intervention.
2. Keep the child calm and in position of comfort (upright, tripod); avoid agitation, supine positioning, throat examination, or use of tongue depressors, as these may precipitate complete airway obstruction.
3. After airway is secured, administer empiric intravenous antibiotics (e.g., third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone, with consideration of vancomycin or ampicillin-sulbactam for MRSA coverage if risk factors exist) to cover likely pathogens including Haemophilus influenzae type b and Streptococcus pneumoniae.
4. Consider corticosteroids to reduce airway edema, though evidence is limited; nebulized epinephrine is not effective for epiglottitis and should not delay airway management.
5. Provide supportive care including mechanical ventilation and ICU monitoring post-intubation; monitor for complications such as sepsis, pneumonia, and epiglottic abscess.
6. Obtain blood cultures after airway is secured to identify the causative organism and tailor antibiotic therapy.
7. Consider transfer to a facility with pediatric ICU and ENT capabilities if not available locally.
8. Address immunization status: the child is not up to date on vaccines, particularly Hib, which increases risk; ensure appropriate antibiotic coverage and plan for catch-up immunization after recovery.
9. Post-extubation care: continue antibiotics, steroids for airway edema, and monitor for complications.
Notes: The thumb sign on X-ray is specific but not always present; clinical diagnosis is paramount. Avoid any oropharyngeal manipulation until the airway is secured. Hypoxia (SpO2 92%) indicates significant airway compromise and need for immediate intervention. Immunization status not up to date increases risk for Hib epiglottitis.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old man is referred by his primary care physician for psychiatric evaluation after presenting with a 2-month history of persistent low mood, loss of interest in activities he previously enjoyed including playing guitar and socializing, insomnia with early morning awakening, decreased appetite with an unintentional 14-pound weight loss, difficulty concentrating at work, and pervasive feelings of worthlessness. He describes his mood as an overwhelming heaviness that does not lift. He has been increasingly isolating from friends and family. He denies suicidal ideation, hallucinations, or delusions. He has no prior psychiatric history. He went through a significant relationship breakup 3 months ago. Vital signs are normal. On mental status examination, he is casually dressed with poor grooming. Psychomotor retardation is present. Speech is soft and slow. Affect is flat. Thought process is linear but impoverished. PHQ-9 score is 22 indicating severe depression.

Sex: Male
Complaint: Persistent low mood, anhedonia, insomnia with early morning awakening, decreased appetite with unintentional 14-pound weight loss, difficulty concentrating, feelings of worthlessness, psychomotor retardation, and social isolation for 2 months following a relationship breakup.
Analysis: The patient meets DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), severe, single episode, without psychotic features. Supporting facts include depressed mood, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, appetite change with significant weight loss, poor concentration, feelings of worthlessness, and psychomotor retardation, all present for 2 months with functional impairment. The PHQ-9 score of 22 confirms severe depression. The absence of suicidal ideation, psychotic features, and normal vital signs indicate no acute emergency, but the severity warrants prompt psychiatric care. Differential considerations include bipolar disorder (depressive episode), adjustment disorder with depressed mood, substance-induced mood disorder, and medical causes such as hypothyroidism, anemia, or vitamin deficiencies. The significant weight loss also warrants evaluation for organic causes (e.g., hyperthyroidism, diabetes, malignancy). The relationship breakup is a major psychosocial stressor, but the severity and duration favor MDD over adjustment disorder.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Laboratory tests including thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), complete blood count (CBC), basic metabolic panel, vitamin B12, folate, and possibly testosterone; urine toxicology screen; assessment for substance use. No neuroimaging indicated without neurological signs.
Conclusion: This is a 35-year-old man with severe Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, without psychotic features, presenting with 2 months of depressive symptoms and significant functional impairment. The condition is non-emergent but requires prompt outpatient psychiatric evaluation and treatment. Medical causes must be excluded, and bipolar disorder must be ruled out before initiating antidepressant monotherapy.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Psychiatry
Recommendations: 
- Refer to psychiatry for comprehensive evaluation and management.
- Screen for bipolar disorder (history of manic/hypomanic episodes) before starting antidepressants to avoid triggering a manic switch.
- Assess for substance use, including alcohol and illicit drugs, as a potential cause or contributor.
- Evaluate family history of mood disorders or suicide.
- Consider collateral information from family or friends to confirm symptom severity and duration.
- Assess functional impairment and social support, as isolation may worsen prognosis; consider safety and support systems.
- Monitor for catatonic features, which may require different treatment.
- Order baseline labs (TSH, CBC, basic metabolic panel, vitamin B12, folate, possibly testosterone, urine toxicology) to rule out medical causes before starting antidepressants.
- The 14-pound weight loss is significant and warrants medical evaluation to rule out organic causes (e.g., malignancy, hyperthyroidism, diabetes) and should be monitored.
- Initiate an SSRI or SNRI at a therapeutic dose with close monitoring; refer for cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT).
- Establish a safety plan and schedule close follow-up within 1-2 weeks to assess response, side effects, and any emergence of suicidal ideation, as energy may improve before mood.
- Reassess PHQ-9 at each visit; monitor weight, sleep, and mood symptoms.
- Document the absence of psychotic features and catatonia to guide treatment choice.
- Consider partial hospitalization if outpatient resources are insufficient given the severity.

Vignette:
A 72-year-old man presents with 3 days of vague periumbilical discomfort that has gradually localized to the right lower quadrant. He reports decreased appetite, mild nausea, and one episode of loose stool. His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, and a total knee replacement. On examination, he is afebrile at 37.2C but appears mildly uncomfortable. Vital signs: HR 92, RR 18, BP 134/78, SpO2 97%. Abdominal exam reveals mild right lower quadrant tenderness without guarding or rebound. WBC is only mildly elevated at 11,200/mcL. CT abdomen with contrast shows a dilated appendix measuring 14 mm with periappendiceal fat stranding and a small contained fluid collection suggestive of early perforation.
winner_protocol:
Age: 72 years

Sex: Male

Complaint: Three days of vague periumbilical discomfort that has gradually localized to the right lower quadrant, accompanied by decreased appetite, mild nausea, and one episode of loose stool.

Analysis: The clinical presentation of periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, nausea, and mild leukocytosis (11,200/mcL) is consistent with acute appendicitis. CT abdomen with contrast confirms the diagnosis by demonstrating a dilated appendix measuring 14 mm with periappendiceal fat stranding and a small contained fluid collection, which is suggestive of early perforation. The patient is afebrile and lacks guarding or rebound, but in an elderly patient with type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease, the absence of fever or marked leukocytosis does not exclude perforation, and mild leukocytosis may underestimate severity. The contained fluid collection may represent a periappendiceal abscess. Main differential considerations include cecal diverticulitis, mesenteric adenitis, Crohn's disease, infectious enterocolitis, ureteral stone, cecal neoplasm, and omental infarction; however, the CT findings are highly specific for appendicitis. The patient's advanced age and comorbidities increase the risk of complications, including sepsis, poor wound healing, and perioperative cardiac events, warranting aggressive and timely management.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Preoperative complete blood count with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel (electrolytes, renal function, glucose), coagulation profile, type and screen, ECG, and cardiac risk assessment given coronary artery disease. Blood cultures and serum lactate may be considered if sepsis is suspected. Serial abdominal examinations and vital sign monitoring are indicated. No further imaging is needed as the CT is diagnostic.

Conclusion: This is acute appendicitis with early perforation, evidenced by a dilated appendix (14 mm), periappendiceal fat stranding, and a small contained fluid collection on CT. The patient requires emergent surgical evaluation and management due to the risk of progression to abscess, diffuse peritonitis, or sepsis, particularly given his age and significant comorbidities.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: General Surgery

Recommendations: Initiate IV fluid resuscitation and keep the patient NPO. Administer broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering gram-negative and anaerobic organisms promptly. Obtain urgent General Surgery consultation for appendectomy (laparoscopic or open), with irrigation and drainage of any abscess. Given the contained fluid collection, non-operative management with antibiotics and percutaneous drainage could be considered in select high-risk cases, but urgent surgery remains the preferred definitive treatment. Optimize perioperative glucose control for diabetes, potentially with insulin therapy while NPO. Perform cardiac risk stratification (ECG, troponin, functional status) given coronary artery disease, continue antianginal medications, and coordinate with anesthesia and cardiology as needed. Admit to the surgical service for urgent operation and postoperative monitoring. Monitor vital signs closely for early sepsis despite the patient being afebrile, and consider lactate measurement. Postoperative care should include early mobilization, DVT prophylaxis, and careful fluid management. The total knee replacement raises the question of antibiotic prophylaxis for prosthetic joint infection, though this is unrelated to the acute appendicitis.

Notes: Elderly patients often have atypical presentations of appendicitis; absence of fever or leukocytosis does not exclude perforation. The one episode of loose stool is nonspecific but can occur in appendicitis. The contained fluid collection may represent a periappendiceal abscess, and non-operative management could be considered in select cases, though surgery remains definitive.

Age: 29
Sex: Male
Complaint: Eye fatigue, dryness, and a mild headache that worsen throughout the workday, with improvement on weekends when screen time is reduced. The patient spends 10–12 hours daily in front of computer screens and often forgets to take breaks.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for computer vision syndrome (digital eye strain) with associated dry eye. The strongest supporting facts are the temporal relationship between prolonged screen use and symptom onset, the improvement with reduced screen time on weekends, the absence of red flags (denied blurred vision, floaters, flashes of light, or eye pain), and a largely normal ocular examination showing only mild conjunctival injection. Visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally, extraocular movements are intact, pupils are equal and reactive, and the anterior segment and fundoscopic exams are normal. The mild conjunctival injection without discharge or pain suggests dry eye rather than infectious conjunctivitis. The absence of corrective lenses and 20/20 acuity makes uncorrected refractive error an unlikely primary cause, though minor errors can still contribute. The headache pattern is consistent with eye strain or tension-type headache; ergonomic factors such as posture should also be considered. Main differential considerations include dry eye syndrome, asthenopia (eye strain), tension headache, accommodative spasm, and migraine; more serious conditions such as retinal detachment, acute angle-closure glaucoma, uveitis, or optic neuritis are ruled out by the absence of red flags and normal examination findings.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None immediately indicated. If symptoms persist despite conservative management, a comprehensive eye examination with tear film assessment (e.g., tear break-up time, Schirmer's test) and refraction may be considered by an ophthalmologist to confirm dry eye and rule out contributing factors.
Conclusion: This is a benign, self-limited condition consistent with computer vision syndrome and associated dry eye. There are no red flags, the examination is essentially normal, and symptoms improve with rest and reduced screen time. The condition is non-urgent and appropriate for self-care with conservative management. Prognosis is excellent with lifestyle modifications.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology
Recommendations: 
- Advise frequent breaks using the 20-20-20 rule (every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds).
- Recommend artificial tears (lubricating eye drops) for dryness.
- Optimize screen ergonomics: proper screen distance and position, adjust screen brightness, reduce glare with anti-glare filters, and ensure adequate lighting.
- Encourage adequate blinking and awareness of blink rate during screen use.
- Recommend reducing total screen time where possible, including short breaks throughout the workday.
- Consider environmental factors such as low humidity, air conditioning, and poor lighting, which may exacerbate symptoms; address these where feasible.
- Consider evaluation for blepharitis or meibomian gland dysfunction as contributing factors to dryness if symptoms persist.
- If symptoms persist or worsen despite conservative measures, further workup for underlying dry eye disease or autoimmune conditions (e.g., Sjögren's syndrome) may be warranted, with referral to ophthalmology.
- Educate the patient that the condition is largely behavioral and environmental, and that prevention is key to avoiding recurrence.
Notes: If symptoms persist despite conservative management, or if new red flags develop (sudden vision loss, severe eye pain, flashes, floaters, or neurological symptoms), further evaluation is warranted. Otherwise, no urgent intervention is needed.

Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Vignette:
A 56-year-old woman with a history of smoking presents to her primary care physician with shortness of breath and cough for several days. Her symptoms began 3 days ago with rhinorrhea. She reports a chronic morning cough productive of white sputum, which has increased over the past 2 days. She has had similar episodes each winter for the past 4 years. She has smoked 1 to 2 packs of cigarettes per day for 40 years and continues to smoke. She denies hemoptysis, chills, or weight loss and has not received any relief from over-the-counter cough preparations.
winner_protocol:
Age: 56
Sex: Female
Complaint: Shortness of breath and cough for several days, with acute worsening of a chronic morning cough productive of white sputum following a 3-day viral prodrome (rhinorrhea); no relief from over-the-counter cough preparations.
Analysis: The patient has a chronic productive cough with recurrent similar episodes each winter for the past 4 years, a 40 pack-year smoking history, and acute worsening of cough and dyspnea after a viral prodrome. These features are classic for an acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis/COPD. The absence of red flags (hemoptysis, chills, weight loss) reduces immediate concern for malignancy, tuberculosis, or severe infection, though they do not exclude them. Main differential considerations include COPD exacerbation, acute bronchitis, pneumonia, asthma, congestive heart failure, and lung cancer (less likely given no hemoptysis or weight loss). The lack of relief from OTC cough preparations is typical for COPD exacerbations and should not delay appropriate prescription therapy.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Spirometry to confirm airflow obstruction and assess severity (FEV1); chest X-ray to exclude pneumonia or other complications; pulse oximetry to assess oxygenation; possibly complete blood count and sputum culture if purulent sputum or signs of bacterial infection are present.
Conclusion: Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis/COPD in a long-term smoker with recurrent winter episodes. The patient is clinically stable with no alarming symptoms, but the worsening dyspnea and cough warrant prompt, non-emergent evaluation and treatment to manage the exacerbation and prevent complications.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: Initiate smoking cessation counseling (the most important intervention; consider pharmacotherapy and referral to a structured smoking cessation program). Prescribe short-acting bronchodilators (e.g., albuterol) for symptom relief; consider a short course of oral corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone for 5–7 days) and antibiotics only if purulent sputum or signs of bacterial infection are present. Ensure adequate hydration and rest. Assess oxygen saturation and respiratory rate to determine severity. Review inhaler technique and provide a written action plan for exacerbations. Update influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations to prevent future exacerbations. Arrange follow-up in 4–6 weeks to reassess symptoms, lung function, and smoking cessation. Discuss pulmonary rehabilitation, screen for depression and anxiety, and evaluate for comorbidities commonly associated with COPD (cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis). Assess for signs of cor pulmonale or right heart failure in advanced disease. Consider alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency testing, though less likely at age 56 with heavy smoking. Discuss advanced care planning. Advise the patient to seek urgent care if symptoms worsen or red flags develop (fever, increased dyspnea, confusion, cyanosis).
Notes: Spirometry results are needed to confirm COPD and grade severity. The 40 pack-year smoking history places the patient at high risk for lung cancer; persistent or worsening symptoms warrant continued vigilance. Absence of hemoptysis, chills, and weight loss reduces but does not exclude malignancy or pneumonia.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.

- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,

Vignette:
A 25-year-old woman presents with 3 days of clear nasal discharge, mild sore throat, and occasional sneezing. She works as a daycare teacher and reports several children in her class have had similar symptoms. She denies fever, cough, dyspnea, ear pain, or facial pressure. On examination, temperature is 37.0°C. The oropharynx shows mild erythema without exudates. Nasal mucosa is mildly edematous with clear discharge. Tympanic membranes are normal bilaterally. Cervical lymph nodes are not enlarged. She is well-appearing and in no distress.
winner_protocol:
Age: 25

Sex: Female

Complaint: Three days of clear nasal discharge, mild sore throat, and occasional sneezing in a daycare teacher with known exposure to children with similar symptoms.

Analysis: The clinical presentation is most consistent with acute viral rhinitis (common cold). Strong supporting facts include clear rhinorrhea, mild sore throat without exudates, sneezing, absence of fever (37.0°C), normal tympanic membranes, and no cervical lymphadenopathy. The patient is well-appearing and in no distress, with no cough, dyspnea, ear pain, or facial pressure, which argues against bacterial sinusitis, otitis media, or lower respiratory involvement. The daycare exposure to children with similar symptoms supports an infectious viral etiology. Main differential considerations include allergic rhinitis (less likely given the absence of itching, sneezing paroxysms, or clear triggers), influenza (less likely given the absence of fever and systemic symptoms), bacterial pharyngitis (less likely given the absence of exudates, fever, and lymphadenopathy), bacterial sinusitis (less likely given clear discharge and no facial pressure), and COVID-19 (can present similarly, though symptoms are mild). No red flags such as respiratory distress, stridor, or toxic appearance are present, reinforcing the benign, self-limited nature of the illness.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical; no laboratory or imaging studies are routinely indicated. If concern arises, a rapid strep test or COVID-19 test could be considered, but they are not indicated based on the low-risk presentation.

Conclusion: This is an uncomplicated acute viral upper respiratory infection (common cold) in a healthy young adult. The illness is self-limited, expected to resolve within 7–10 days, and requires no diagnostic testing, antibiotics, or specialist referral. Management is supportive, with attention to transmission prevention given the daycare setting.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate

Subclinical specialization: General Medicine

Recommendations: Provide supportive care including rest, adequate hydration, saline nasal spray, and over-the-counter analgesics (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen) for sore throat if needed; over-the-counter decongestants may be considered if nasal congestion is bothersome. Antibiotics are not indicated. Advise the patient on hand hygiene and respiratory etiquette to prevent transmission, particularly given her role as a daycare teacher. Consider COVID-19 testing given the daycare exposure and current pandemic context, though symptoms are mild. Assess pregnancy status, as it may affect medication choices (e.g., decongestants). Advise return precautions: she should seek re-evaluation if she develops high fever, worsening symptoms, new symptoms (e.g., cough, ear pain, facial pain, difficulty breathing, severe sore throat, stridor, neck stiffness, or rash), or if symptoms persist beyond 10 days, which could indicate a secondary bacterial infection or other complication. No routine follow-up is needed.

Notes: The absence of fever, exudates, and cervical lymphadenopathy reduces the likelihood of bacterial pharyngitis. Clear nasal discharge and sneezing are more consistent with viral rhinitis than with bacterial sinusitis, which typically involves purulent discharge and facial pain. Normal tympanic membranes rule out otitis media. Allergic rhinitis could be considered if symptoms persist beyond the typical viral course.

Vignette:
A 5-year-old boy is brought in by his mother who noticed multiple itchy red bumps on his arms and legs after he spent the afternoon playing outside in the backyard. The bumps appeared over the past 24 hours. He has been scratching but the mother reports no significant swelling beyond the immediate area of each bump. He denies fever, joint pain, or any recent travel. On examination, there are approximately 8 to 10 small erythematous papules, each 3 to 5 mm in diameter, scattered on the bilateral forearms and lower legs. Several have small central puncta. There is no surrounding cellulitis, lymphangitis, or regional lymphadenopathy.

Age: 5 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Multiple itchy red bumps on the arms and legs that appeared over the past 24 hours after playing outside in the backyard; the child has been scratching but reports no fever, joint pain, or significant swelling beyond the immediate area of each bump.
Analysis: The presentation of approximately 8 to 10 small (3–5 mm) erythematous papules with central puncta scattered on the bilateral forearms and lower legs, appearing after outdoor play in an otherwise well child, is classic for papular urticaria (an insect bite hypersensitivity reaction). The central puncta strongly suggest arthropod bites, and the distribution on exposed extremities supports this. The absence of fever, joint pain, significant swelling, cellulitis, lymphangitis, and regional lymphadenopathy effectively excludes systemic infection, severe local infection, and anaphylaxis. The main differential considerations include contact dermatitis, folliculitis, scabies, viral exanthem, and impetigo, but the morphology (central puncta), exposure history, and lack of systemic features make insect bites the most consistent diagnosis. Scratching raises the risk of secondary bacterial infection (impetigo or cellulitis), which should be monitored. No travel history reduces the likelihood of exotic infections, though endemic tick-borne illnesses remain a theoretical consideration if tick exposure is possible.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. This is a clinical diagnosis; no laboratory, imaging, or other studies are indicated. Skin scraping or biopsy could be considered only if lesions become atypical or fail to respond to symptomatic management.
Conclusion: This is a benign, self-limited case of papular urticaria (insect bite reaction) in a 5-year-old boy. The condition is non-urgent, requires no diagnostic testing, and is appropriate for home-based symptomatic management with monitoring for secondary infection. The expected course is resolution over days to weeks, with possible recurrence upon repeated insect exposure.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Manage symptomatically at home. Apply cool compresses to the lesions to reduce itching and inflammation. Administer oral antihistamines for pruritus (topical antihistamines should be avoided due to potential sensitization). Apply a low-potency topical corticosteroid (e.g., hydrocortisone) to the affected areas. Advise keeping the child's nails short and discouraging scratching to prevent secondary bacterial infection; maintain good hygiene. Educate the caregiver on identifying and addressing the insect source (e.g., pets, bedding, standing water, other household members with similar lesions) and on using insect repellent and protective clothing to prevent further bites. No antibiotics are indicated unless secondary infection develops. Advise the caregiver to return for re-evaluation if the child develops fever, spreading erythema, increasing pain, pus or drainage from lesions, lymphangitis, regional lymphadenopathy, blistering, mucosal involvement, or any systemic symptoms (e.g., respiratory distress, facial swelling), which would suggest secondary infection, a systemic reaction, or a more serious process. Primary care or pediatrics can manage this condition; dermatology referral is reserved for atypical, persistent, or refractory cases.
Notes: Papular urticaria is a hypersensitivity reaction to insect bites and may recur with repeated exposure; new lesions may appear over time and the condition can persist for weeks. The specific insect (e.g., mosquito, flea, chigger) is not identified in this case. If lesions become vesicular, necrotic, or painful, consider other arthropod bites (e.g., brown recluse spider) or infection. The absence of fever, joint pain, and lymphadenopathy helps exclude systemic inflammatory or infectious conditions.

Vignette:
A 77-year-old man reports a 5-day history of burning and aching pain on the right side of his chest. This is followed by the development of erythema and a maculopapular rash in this painful area, accompanied by headache and malaise. The rash progressed to develop clusters of clear vesicles for 3 to 5 days, evolving through stages of pustulation, ulceration, and crusting.
winner_protocol:
Age: 77 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: A 5-day history of burning and aching pain on the right side of the chest, followed by erythema and a maculopapular rash in the same area, which progressed to clusters of clear vesicles over 3 to 5 days, evolving through pustulation, ulceration, and crusting. The rash is accompanied by headache and malaise.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for herpes zoster (shingles) due to reactivation of varicella-zoster virus. The strongest supporting facts are the unilateral dermatomal distribution of pain preceding the rash in an older adult, the evolution of the rash through vesicular, pustular, ulcerative, and crusting stages, and the associated systemic symptoms of headache and malaise. The right-sided chest location suggests involvement of a thoracic dermatome, which is common and typically not associated with ophthalmic complications. The main differential considerations include herpes simplex virus infection, contact dermatitis, impetigo, cellulitis, and, because the pain precedes the rash in the chest area, rarely acute coronary syndrome. The unilateral dermatomal pattern and vesicular evolution strongly favor herpes zoster. Age 77 is a significant risk factor for postherpetic neuralgia and more severe disease, and immunosenescence increases the risk of reactivation and complications.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Clinical diagnosis is usually sufficient; no additional testing is routinely required. If the presentation is atypical, PCR or direct immunofluorescence (DFA) of vesicular fluid, or a Tzanck smear, can be used for confirmation. Serology for VZV antibodies may be considered in uncertain cases. Consider HIV testing if risk factors for immunocompromise are present.
Conclusion: This is a case of herpes zoster (shingles) in a 77-year-old man, presenting with unilateral thoracic dermatomal pain and a characteristic vesicular rash that has progressed through pustulation, ulceration, and crusting. The condition requires non-emergent care but should be evaluated promptly, ideally within 72 hours of rash onset, to initiate antiviral therapy, which reduces acute pain and the risk of postherpetic neuralgia. No red flags for emergency care (e.g., ophthalmic involvement, disseminated rash, immunocompromised status, or secondary bacterial infection) are present in the case.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Initiate antiviral therapy (e.g., valacyclovir, famciclovir, or acyclovir) within 72 hours of rash onset to reduce viral shedding, accelerate healing, and decrease the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia. Provide analgesics for pain control and supportive wound care; consider adjunctive corticosteroids in certain cases. Assess immunization status for the herpes zoster vaccine, as vaccination is recommended for prevention in older adults. Evaluate for immunocompromising conditions (e.g., malignancy, HIV, immunosuppressive therapy), as immunocompromised patients may have atypical presentations or disseminated disease requiring more aggressive management. Monitor for complications, particularly postherpetic neuralgia (a common complication in older adults), secondary bacterial superinfection (which may necessitate antibiotics), and scarring. Arrange follow-up for ongoing pain management and assessment of healing. If the rash involves the tip of the nose or the eye, urgent ophthalmology referral is needed to prevent corneal damage. Note that the pain preceding the rash can mimic cardiac ischemia, especially in the chest area.
Notes: Age 77 is a significant risk factor for postherpetic neuralgia and more severe disease; early antiviral treatment may reduce this risk. The presence of headache and malaise may indicate systemic involvement, but without additional signs, it is not a red flag for emergency. Monitor for dissemination, especially if the patient is immunocompromised.

EMS administered 10 mg of intramuscular midazolam en route, but seizure activity persisted. Her past medical history includes focal epilepsy diagnosed at age 16, treated with levetiracetam. criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.
